#1541. Ferrero sets Juventus ambition to be what it once was, as €200m capital raise runs

Juventus president Gianluca Ferrero set out the leadership's view of the rebuild at the Brussels launch of the club's European Union fan club. He spoke while a capital raise of about €200m is open and a UEFA settlement limits spending.

Juventus president Gianluca Ferrero went to Brussels on 18 November with a clear message for supporters. Restoring the club to its former self is its absolute ambition, he said, adding that the club is following the path set out by its chief executive and is confident this can happen. He spoke at the opening of the Juventus Official Fan Club European Union, which is chaired by MEP Sandro Gozi. The timing gives the statement weight.

The new supporters’ club opened at the Iosono il Piemonte event space. Its stated purpose is to link Juventus supporters with the institutional centre of Europe.

Before the opening, the delegation went to the European Parliament with Gozi. Chief Club Affairs Officer Giorgio Chiellini led the group alongside Ferrero. Piedmont regional president Alberto Cirio attended the opening, as did MEPs who have joined the fan club.

The visit showed Chiellini’s work on the club’s relations with institutions and European football. It also gives supporters an official club in Brussels.

The financial backdrop is demanding. Juventus posted a consolidated loss of €66m for 2025/26. On 12 November, the board approved the offer, using part of the €250m authority granted by shareholders at the extraordinary meeting on 3 November.

The offer involves up to 208.5m new shares at €0.96 each. Shareholders can buy one new share for every two they hold. The price is 28.36% below the theoretical ex-rights price, based on that day’s share price. The remaining €50m of the authority can be used in later financial years, depending on the club’s financial needs and investment plans.

The spending limits come from UEFA. European football’s governing body fined Juventus €20m for breaking the football earnings rule. Of that amount, €14m is conditional. The club agreed a three-year settlement with annual targets. It also faces limits on registering new players on its UEFA List A.

Those are the limits within which Ferrero’s ambition must be pursued. Any improvement in the squad has to fit within the annual targets agreed with UEFA.

Subscription rights can be traded on Euronext Milan until 25 November, and the offer closes on 1 December 2026.

#1540. Martin Odegaard bails out comically wasteful Arsenal

For much of this sticky night in Naples, Arsenal appeared to be starting the new Champions League campaign the same way they finished the last one: by erroneously smashing the ball into the stands behind the goal.

Memories of Gabriel Magalhães’s ballooned penalty in the final against Paris St-Germain remain fresh in the mind, and here his team-mates were lining up to produce their own versions. Bukayo Saka and Piero Hincapié, especially, delivered astonishing misses which were closer to entering orbit than the opposition net.

Thankfully for Arsenal, though, there was one player who was in no mood to relive the frustration of that shoot-out loss 14 weeks ago. Martin Odegaard has started this season in truly fabulous form and here he scored a truly fabulous late goal, fizzed into the corner from range, to cap another inventive individual performance and earn three points for his team.

Great play 😮‍💨Martin Ødegaard rounds off a wonderful passing move for Arsenal 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FrH6gW8Ak4

In five matches this season, Odegaard has already scored four goals. That is three more than he managed in the whole of last season. The Arsenal captain is fit again and he is flowing. As ever, when Odegaard flows, Arsenal flow.

“That’s what we need, the players with that mindset to decide the game and play with that personality,” said Mikel Arteta. “He has got that edge. He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games.”

In the end it was a thoroughly deserved victory for the Premier League side, who were superior to Napoli in every department. Were it not for their comically bad finishing, they would have guaranteed the result long before Odegaard’s 75th-minute strike.

Their expected goals figure suggested they should have scored more than four goals, compared to Napoli’s 0.22. In total, they registered 26 shots – the most of any Arsenal team on record in a single Champions League match, and the most on record a Napoli team has ever faced.

“With the amount of chances we generated, the scoreline has to reflect a very different result,” said Arteta. “The number of players that got into this situation, the amount of situations that we generated in various ways was something that pleased me a lot.”

There was, almost inevitably, another clean sheet for Arteta’s side. They had the best defence in the Champions League last season, conceding only seven goals in 15 matches, and they were largely untroubled here. Ezri Konsa was once again excellent, in only his second start for the club. He successfully wrapped up Rasmus Hojlund, the former Manchester United centre-forward, and was as calm in possession as the absent William Saliba would have been. A potential injury to right-back Ben White was a concern, though.

The Champions League is the one that Arsenal have never won and, you suspect, the one that Arteta really wants. Success in this competition would elevate Arsenal to a higher level as a club and fully establish Arteta as one of the great coaching minds of his generation.

To lose last season’s final in such painful circumstances clearly hurt the Arsenal manager, who was visibly distraught after that shoot-out defeat despite the obvious delight of winning the Premier League title. If you could give him the choice between retaining the league this season or leading Arsenal to their first European Cup, he would surely pick the latter.

Arsenal have now won THIRTEEN UCL League Phase games in a row 🔴🔥 pic.twitter.com/UmcfMYO13r

A trip to Naples in the first round of the league phase made for a lovely opening tie: atmospheric, intense and competitive. Napoli have had a difficult start to their campaign, losing two of three Serie A games so far, but they possess real quality and have a top manager in Massimiliano Allegri.

Even at the age of 35, the great Kevin De Bruyne still has power in his boots and schemes in his mind. When he tested Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya from range in the first half, it would have triggered horrible flashbacks in the minds of the travelling supporters. In his previous 17 starts against Arsenal for Manchester City, De Bruyne had scored eight goals and registered four assists. Thankfully for Arsenal, it was the only moment in which De Bruyne really threatened.

Throughout this game, Arsenal moved the ball around with precision and purpose. They created an extraordinary amount of chances, with Saka and Hincapié missing the best of them. Saka’s effort in the first half, when one-v-one with the goalkeeper, was strangely erratic. Hincapié’s opportunity, meanwhile, was laughable. Two yards out from goal, he somehow put the ball onto the running track that surrounds the pitch at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.

Despite all the wasted chances, Arsenal kept going. Odegaard, in particular, kept probing. His goal was gorgeous: a swift exchange of passes between him, White and Christos Tzolis resulted in the Arsenal captain firing his effort from the edge of the area. Delicate build-up, ferocious finish.

In keeping with the theme of the night, Arsenal should have scored more. Noni Madueke, for example, missed a one-v-one when it seemed like he had all the time in the world. But Odegaard’s intervention eventually proved to be enough, as he once again stood forward as Arsenal’s match-winner.

That’s all from us, but we’ll be back tomorrow night to bring you Man Utd’s return to the Champions League against Sabah!

"I think the chemistry, especially in the front players, has been exceptional." ✨Mikel Arteta tells @AnitaNnekaJones how impressed he's been by the connection between Martin Ødegaard and Christos Tzolis 🤝 pic.twitter.com/J6VOAMk4Lm

Arsenal extend their #UCL unbeaten streak 👏 pic.twitter.com/wFBga6lNrN

"We missed so many big chances"Mikel Arteta shares his thoughts after Arsenal's victory over Napoli 💭🎙️ @DannyJamieson | 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/zT2bHcPoiH

Before all of that, Arsenal will now have to turn their attention to the Stadium of Light as they travel to Sunderland on Saturday.

They then face Ipswich Town in the EFL Cup on Tuesday night, before travelling to Brighton on the weekend.

Tue, November 24: Borussia Dortmund (H) 8pm

“Everything runs through Martin Odegaard,” said Cole on TNT Sports. “He can stand still and find space. He is at the peak of his powers and it is beautiful to watch.

“You can’t help but love watching him play his football.”

Plenty of praise for Martin Odegaard on TNT, with former Arsenal man Martin Keown heralding the captain’s behaviour.

“He’s setting an example to his players. He’s fitter, he’s hungry, and he did his talking on the pitch. He came good for his team.”

Couple that with his impressive chemistry with new arrival Christos Tzolis, and there is a lot of goal-scoring potential there this season. Three of the winger’s four assists have been for his captain, and we’re barely a month into the season.

The action has concluded around Europe tonight so here are your final scores from this week’s second night of European football:

Napoli did not register a shot on target in that second half, and it is clear how much Arsenal just dominated to keep the pressure on.

It could easily have been three or four goals for Arsenal had they had better finishing, but either way, they did not let their heads go down.

They kept pushing to see out the result and got the job done. Arteta will be very happy with that away result.

This has not been Arsenal’s most clinical performance but they got the job done.

Here is the goal that won it for them, courtesy of their captain:

Great play 😮‍💨Martin Ødegaard rounds off a wonderful passing move for Arsenal 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FrH6gW8Ak4

Napoli are fighting, but Arsenal hold fast.

Milinković-Savić waves his players downfield for the final minute but Olivera can’t control the ball well.

Four minutes will be added on here as Napoli are being urged on by their fans.

Arsenal need to hold onto the ball and manage the game intelligently here. Zubimendi goes in for a challenge though and hauls down his man, and Napoli get the ball back. Odegaard goes into the book for his protests.

Napoli again, still trying to get their goal and De Bruyne gives them a chance with a through ball to David Neres, but the striker can’t get on the ball.

Arsenal are almost caught as the ball falls to De Bruyne on the left of the box, with a clear look at Raya in goal, but the Belgian crosses the ball thinking he’s got a team-mate there to put it away but there is no one and it is a huge let-off for Arsenal.

Napoli with every man forward lose the ball and suddenly Zubimendi finds himself on the break. With Madueke on his right, he feeds the winger who gets into space in the box to be one-on-one with Milinković-Savić. But the Arsenal man hesitates and the keeper spreads himself, blocking Madueke’s eventual shot. He can’t turn around to get on the rebound and cuts is back for Tzolis, whose own shot is then blocked.

With just a few minutes to go, Arsenal make their final change.

Ben White appeared to be in a little bit of discomfort a few minutes ago. He’s now been replaced by Martin Zubimendi for the final 10 minutes of this game. Declan Rice appears to have moved to right-back.

Martin Odegaard has played some outstanding football tonight (again) and that is an absolutely outstanding goal. The delicacy of the build-up and then the ferocity of the finish. Four goals in five games for Odegaard this season.

There will be alarm bells ringing for Allegri and Napoli, as they are heading for their third defeat on the trot. They have not created much of anything in this second half and you have to imagine that Arsenal will now make life very difficult for them.

To be exact, they have had a grand total of one shot in the second half.

Napoli will have to push now, and make more changes, bringing on Lorenzo Lucca and David Neres for Rasmus Hojlund and Stanislav Lobotka.

The breakthrough comes and of course it is Odegaard! Finally they get their moment, hacing recycled the ball on the edge of the area.

Rice just passes it out to him off a nice ball from Tzolis and the captain rifles a low shot into the far bottom corner.

Rice loses the ball in midfield and fouls Olivera as he tries to recover it.

Before they take the free kick though, Arsenal make more changes. Kai Havertz and Noni Madueke come on for Gyokeres and Saka.

Guimaraes to Saka before the winger sends the ball back to Odegaard on the edge of the box. He lifts a ball into the centre of the box where there are a lot of bodies, but Tzolis snatches at it and sends the ball into the rafters.

Sums up the game so far really for Arsenal.

There is definitely a goal in here somewhere. Napoli are still waiting and searching for their goal, and Arsenal will keep throwing shots at the wall until something sticks.

There are the subs, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze are the ones to make way.

Christos Tzolis and Bruno Guimaraes getting ready to come on.

At the same time, Favasuli makes a neat little run on the right trying to get to the touchline and pull the ball back, but Raya is able to pick it up easily.

That was almost it for Napoli, Hojlund with a great run in behind. He gets into the box one-on-one against his defender as Raya retreats. The challenge is perfectly timed though as he tries to get his shot off and the ball goes spinning off to the side.

Neither side are looking clinical in front of goal though as Arsenal take the ball down the other end, and Declan Rice can only send another shot over the bar.

Saka tries to take another chance on the edge of the box, but he loses the ball.

Napoli try to seize their moment on the break, with Favasuli releasing down the left side. He looks for Hojlund in the middle of the field, but his cross is just not good enough and Raya comes out to collect the high ball.

Politano and Alisson Santos make way for Antonio Vergara and Constantino Favasuli.

Though the hosts came out on the front foot, it has been all Arsenal since then, so Allegri will be hoping these changes can shift the momentum.

Alisson Santos gets past White on the sideline, and makes the run down the left. He tries to find De Bruyne making the run in the middle but it is intercepted and Arsenal take the ball back up the field.

Napoli are getting ready to make some changes.

Arsenal probing again, with Rice, Saka, Odegaard and White exchanging passes on the right edge of the box. Saka tries a low ball in but it’s blocked before it gets to Gyokeres.

Napoli are sitting so deep, you have to assume they are just waiting for an opportunity to counter. Even so, Arsenal are doing well to keep the ball moving around and try and find space. The hosts are really trying not to concede first.

Another wasted chance for Arsenal! Great play from Odegaard lifting a little ball into the centre of the box, which is flicked on towards goal. It falls to Hincapié in the six-yard box but as he tries to poke it into the goal, the Ecuadorian sends it flying over the bar.

Napoli have every man behind the ball right now as Arsenal get some possession.

Arsenal’s turn now, as White gets himself into a good position on the right side of the box, exchanging passes with Odegaard and Saka.

Saka tries to send a ball into the box, but it’s blocked and sent out the sideline as Napoli remain disciplined and shut down the space.

That momentum falls apart for Napoli as Oliveira fouls Gyokeres as the strikers comes in to defend.

Napoli are starting with some pressure here..

Napoli have changed their keepers at half-time. Meret received some treatment in the first half and has been taken off, replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic. It’s his first appearance of the season.

Arsenal with the better of the first half, but unable to find the breakthrough.

Liverpool have equalised at Anfield after Marcos Llorente put Atlético Madrid ahead. Dominik Szoboszlai is the man to put the ball in the back of the net – to the great relief of Andoni Iraola I’m sure.

Reigning champions PSG are 3-0 up against Slovan, with a quick double coming from Mr Ballon D’or himself, Ousmane Dembélé. Ferran Torres scored the third.

Sporting vs Galatasaray also level at 1-1 so it’s really all to play for in the next 45 minutes. Stay tuned!

That’s the final action of the half, and nothing separates the two sides at the break. Both with three shots on target, though Arsenal have taken 13 shots to Napoli’s four.

Both teams could have stolen a goal to take the lead, but they will have to wait for the second period for the opportunity.

Arsenal get a corner which is delivered really well to the far post, but as it’s headed in, there is no space for White to turn and shoot from the six-yard box. He tries to lay it off for Hincapié but Meret gets low to grab it.

Arsenal have created more than enough chances to be three or four goals clear here. That miss by Saka was the best one yet, and the England winger will be in disbelief at the spooned nature of his finish. It looked a certain goal. Shocker.

Arsenal get another great chance as Odegaard sends a perfect ball to Saka as he makes the run into the box on the right side. The winger stays onside but Lobotka does enough to put him off and Saka sends it over the bar.

Napoli are first into the book as Gilmour fouls Eze 35 yards out.

Arsenal take the free kick but end up passing the ball around the edge of the box. Eventually Odegaard lifts a high ball into the box, but Meret punches it away confidently.

Konsa does really well to hold up Alisson Santos as he makes a very speedy run down the left, keeping him from sending a ball into the box.

The game is opening up now, as Saka makes a run of his own down the right, with Gyokeres in the box but Napoli keep tight and Rrahmani does well to stop the ball reaching the striker.

A good save from Raya as Hojlund again feeds the wings from the centre of the field. Politano makes a great run in from the right side with the ball and takes a curling shot with his left foot on the edge of the box.

Arsenal’s keeper collects and then minutes later his side have a shot of their own, but Saka can only send it over the bar.

Saka again gets enough time on the right edge of the box to send a low ball to Rice in the right corner. His shot goes over the bar and we’re having an impromptu drinks break as Meret gets some treatment.

Treat yourself to a hydration break of your own.

Napoli coming close as Hojlund fed in the centre, one-on-one with Konsa, trying to turn at the top of the box. He dinks the ball into the path of the running De Bruyne, whose shot is blocked by Konsa, who scrambles back quickly.

Hincapié sends a cross in from the left which almost catches Meret out at the near post as the keeper scrambles across to push it away.

Now it’s Napoli’s turn as Lobotka sends a long ball down the left to Alisson Santos, who sends a great cross in to the box. Konsa just does enough to put him off and it meets Rice in the centre of the box, for the midfielder to clear.

Saka comes in again on his left foot, with a series of short passes between Odegaard and Rice, but his shot is blocked as two defenders shut him down.

Another attempt for Arsenal as Odegaard gets forward and passes to Eze on the left wing. He drives in and takes a shot with his right foot from just inside the box, but he drags it wide of the target.

Good start to this game. Plenty going on. Arsenal look dangerous and capable of pinning Napoli deep into their own half, but the Italians have threatened on the break. De Bruyne’s shot from range would have triggered some nasty flashbacks for the Arsenal fans but, thankfully for them, it was straight at Raya.

Great chance from Arsenal as Eze pulls away at the back post and connects with the ball to send a header into the box. Merino connects with a diving header of his own but it’s straight at Meret and tipped over the bar.

Arsenal again biding their time until Rice plays a neat ball to White on the right edge of the boxm which he lifts into the box. No one around to do anything with it and Meret collects.

Arsenal being patient on the edge of the box moving the ball around, but eventually it breaks down with Eze losing the ball and then fouling De Bruyne as he tries to break away.

The Napoli players feel that should have been a card.

Di Lorenzo again looks to find space down the centre of the field but sends the ball out to Politano again on the right wing, who lofts a very high ball towards the back post but Raya collects with confidence.

Di Lorenzo makes a great run onto a long ball on the left side, racing down the sideline. He sends a ball across to find De Bruyne in the centre of the field, and the midfielder takes a great shot, which Raya can’t hold on to. White reacts to clear but Napoli are having a good spell.

Politano is the next to force a save from the Arsenal keeper with a shot from the right corner of the box, keeping their visitors very much on their toes.

Arsenal dominating possession in the early stages, just testing the Napoli defence. The stadium is quite quiet and we can hear the travelling fans declaring their love for their team.

Free kick for the visitors as Eze is fouled 40 yards out. Odegaard takes and sends a high ball into the centre of the box, which Gabriel can’t quite control.

Arsenal come again as Gyokeres sends a cross into the box from the left and Saka tries an overhead kick but it is straight into the centre of the goal and Meret has little trouble.

Rice again but the keeper comes to collect and sets the counter free.

Hojlund makes a great run and feeds Alisson Santos on the left side. He tries to cut in but is well marked by White and he can only send his shot over the bar from inside the box.

Arsenal get their first corner as Eze finds himself in a central position at the top of the box, and plays neat one-two with Gyokeres, but his shot takes a big deflection.

Rice goes to the corner flag, and sends in a good ball, headed out by Napoli for another corner.

Arsenal probing on the right wing, with White, Odegaard and Saka overlapping nicely. The captain feeds White and he passes in a neat little ball to Saka just inside the box. He tries a shot, but it’s blocked.

Napoli are getting back very quickly when Arsenal are pressing.

Marín sends a nice high ball across the field to find Politano on the right side. He feeds De Bruyne on the edge of the box and the Belgian tries a shot at Raya, curling it with his right foot, but with not much on it, Raya collects in the middle of goal.

Both teams getting little spells on the ball to get going.

Arsenal are keeping tight as Napoli try and play the ball out from the back and the long ball out to Hojlund is easily collected for Raya.

You can hear the Arsenal fans in loud voice, accompanied by plenty of jeers and whistles from the home fans.

The players are lining up around the centre circle, with a minute of silence for the victims of the tragedy in Nepal.

I wrote a little while ago that it was an unpleasantly warm evening in Naples. I now want to revise that comment. It’s nastily hot, and it’s getting worse. The air is thick (27 degrees and 74 per cent humidity, according to my weather app) and I can’t imagine it will be easy for the players.

As the players line up in the tunnel, here are the full teams in black and white:

Subs: Kepa, Meslier, Tzolis, Madueke, Havertz, Calafiori, Zubimendi, Lewis-Skelly, Dowman, Salmon

Barcelona managed to get five past Feyenoord, with recently departed Arsenal striker Gabriel Jesus scoring the last goal minutes after coming on.

“Every game starts at 0-0, but clearly Arsenal are favourites. We’ll need to show our strength and ability to be competitive. We’ll approach the game with determination and pride as we try to get a positive result.

“We have to turn over a new leaf. We face a different challenge tomorrow. We’ll need to put in a technically excellent performance and be able to defend better than we did against Como and Inter.”

These two sides haven’t met since the 2018-19 Europa League quarter-finals, when Alexandre Lacazette sent Arsenal through to the last four with a cracking goal.

Arsenal have only travelled to Naples once in the Champions League, back in 2013, which saw the home side win 2-0 and then Arsenal captain Mikel Arteta get sent off with two yellows. Arsenal still made it out of the group stages that year, helped by their own 2-0 win when the Italians came to N5.

“We know what this competition means to all of us, the experience of last year as well, so we need to start with the first game in a really, really tough place, but really excited to start the campaign.

“It will be a really tough place, I’ve been in that stadium before, I know the atmosphere they create, their record at home is really, really strong. They have a very experienced manager, a lot of players that played in the league as well, so we know the challenge ahead. We are prepared and we’re ready to go.”

Two matches kicked off at 5.45pm, and with just under half an hour to go:

The visitors are still without Cristhian Mosquera, who picked up an injury against Aston Villa, and Jurrien Timber – though the right-back has rejoined first-team training and travelled with the squad to Italy. William Saliba remains their only long-term absentee as he recovers from a back injury.

Naples have a few more players out of action. As well as McTominay, centre-back Alessandro Buongiorno is still sidelined following a knee procedure over summer and Andre-Frank Zambo Anguissa is missing with a groin injury.

Strikers Giovane and David Neres are dealing with hernia and knee problems respectively, while youngster Luca Marianucci is on his way back after a knee injury in pre-season.

Napoli have not started the season particularly well, losing two of their three Serie A games so far. But they do have a player who has a long history of hurting Arsenal: the great Kevin De Bruyne. The former Manchester City midfielder has been directly involved in 12 goals in his last 17 starts against Arsenal across all competitions (8 goals, 4 assists), including five in his most recent three (3 goals, 2 assists). Now 35 though, he is not the force he once was.

Mikel Arteta’s side were the only team who didn’t lose a single game in normal time in this competition last season, and also conceded only seven goals all season — the fewest of any team in the competition, despite the fact they played 15 matches.

Mikel Arteta has made four changes to the team that defeated Chelsea on Sunday. Piero Hincapie comes in for Riccardo Calafiori, Mikel Merino for Myles Lewis-Skelly, Eberechi Eze for Christos Tzolis and Viktor Gyokeres for Kai Havertz.

#1539. A very positive record: Luca Pairetto will officiate Milan’s game against Frosinone

Luca Pairetto has been assigned to the game between AC Milan and Frosinone on Sunday evening, which is good news for the Rossoneri.

Ruben Amorim and his men will be looking to make it three consecutive wins against Frosinone, after beating Inter and Genoa before the international break. It might not be such an easy task, though, as admitted by the gaffer himself in his press conference.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Frosinone have indeed started the season well, currently sitting in sixth place, and they don’t really have anything to lose from their trip to San Siro. Only something to gain, which can always make things tricky for the favourite.

Given the above, as always, Milan will be hoping for good officiating to keep the away side from disrupting the play too much. The Italian Referees Association, also known as AIA, announced the referees for this weekend’s game a few days ago and for the Rossoneri, it will be Luca Pairetto.

The 42-year-old is definitely one of the more experienced referees around, even if he has never reached the heights of some of his colleagues. In any case, he has officiated 12 games involving Milan so far and the record is positive: 9 wins, 2 draws and 1 defeat.

It’s been a while since he last officiated a Milan game, though, as we have to go back to the 2024-25 season. The Rossoneri played Empoli and beat them 2-0, courtesy of goals from Rafael Leao and Santiago Gimenez.

Despite the win, the game wasn’t without controversy. A red card was not given to Empoli despite a reckless challenge, and Fikayo Tomori was then given a second yellow when the whole sequence should have been stopped due to offside.

However, most of those errors were made by VAR or the assistant referee and not Pairetto himself.

#1538. Man City MUST stop the rot, old rivals Chelsea and Leeds set for Stamford Bridge blockbuster and Mauricio Pochettino's baptism of fire: SEVEN reasons we're excited for the return of the Premier League

Published: 17:05 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:05 EST, 17 November 2026

After a thrilling international break that saw England record an historic 3-2 win over Spain our focus returns to the Premier League.

And what a weekend we have coming up. Old gaffers in new colours, fierce rivalries and some seminal fixtures in the context of the whole season.

With so much to look forward to this weekend, Daily Mail Sport looks over the key reasons to be excited for the return of the world's most electric league.

After a flying start to the campaign Manchester City have begun to run into serious problems under Enzo Maresca and have lost their last three Premier League games on the trot.

And after a particularly humiliating defeat away to Nottingham Forest, who hadn't scored at home before the Cityzens' visit, Maresca and his squad will be desperate for three points especially with champions Arsenal now six points clear.

City have a good opportunity to turn things around, though, as they host a Fulham side who have endured a terrible run of form against Saturday’s opponents. In fact, the Cottagers have failed to beat City in their last 20 Premier League meetings - a run stretching back 14 years.

But, as ever in the Premier League, nothing is guaranteed and Alvaro Arbeloa’s side are showing promising signs - having enjoyed an unbeaten run in their past four games.

Enzo Maresca's side started in scintillating form but have lost their last three games

Bonfire night has only just passed but don’t be surprised to see fireworks in west London on Saturday as old rivals Chelsea and Leeds do battle at Stamford Bridge.

After comfortably surviving in their returning year last season, Leeds have kicked on and have quietly emerged as a strong contender for European football. Daniel Farke’s side currently sit ninth, just two points off fifth place Chelsea.

The Blues on the other hand have endured a stuttering, frustrating start to the season. Xabi Alonso’s heralded front three of Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro have showcased their terrifying attacking prowess, but the Blues boss’ mystifying tinkering, plus inconsistent performances, has seen his side drop points against Spurs and Sunderland.

However, form will go out of the window as this rivalry - 55 years in the making - is reignited

Chelsea will be hoping for a repeat of their 6-3 win over Leeds in the league cup this season but Daniel Farke's men will not be as easy to get past in the league

After Pierre Sage’s dismal start to life in south London, the Crystal Palace board did not hang around and gave the Frenchman the boot after just five months in charge.

And the Eagles have made sure to replace him with someone who has Premier League pedigree, Thomas Frank.

Now while recent memories of the Danish gaffer are almost universally negative it is easy to forget that before his calamitous stint at Tottenham he worked wonders down in west London for Brentford.

And he has every chance of doing the same at Selhurst Park. The job will be far from easy as his new team currently sit rock bottom of the league, but considering Frank’s high pressing and wide set playstyle, Palace’s squad looks a good fit for the Dane.

His first game back will be a tough test, away to Frank Lampard’s resurgent Coventry, but Frank - and the travelling Palace contingent - will be hoping for a new manager bounce in the east Midlands.

Thomas Frank returns to London to take charge of a struggling Crystal Palace side

With City faltering and Liverpool and Chelsea failing to hit their stride, the Premier League title race is fast developing into a one-horse competition - and Mikel Arteta will not care one bit.

The Spaniard’s well-oiled machine looks near impossible to stop but as Brighton proved before the last international break, they are not infallible and are set for a tough test returning from the latest break.

The Gunners travel to St James’ Park to take on Newcastle in what promises to be another thriller.

In years past the trip up north has proved to be a banana skin for Arsenal and Arteta, losing four out of their last six games there.

However, Newcastle fans fear their side are fast becoming a fading force and the trip to the North East isn’t perhaps as intimidating as it once was. After all, the Gunners picked up a stoppage time win there last season on their way to the title.

Mikel Arteta's side are hitting their stride but face a tough test at St James' Park

The surprise package of the season has undoubtedly been Fabian Hurzeler’s high-flying Seagulls who are perched in second place after 10 excellent games.

They remain the only side to have beaten the champions Arsenal and are the league’s top scorers by five goals. They are efficient, fun to watch and have scored a plethora of absolute scorchers this season, but the question on everyone’s lips is: can they keep it up?

History would suggest that overperforming teams tend to settle into the pack after a fast start, and end up battling it out for a coveted spot in a lesser European competition.

But somehow this year it feels different. Brighton appear to have everything they might need to maintain this form and seriously challenge for a Champions League place.

The squad has depth and dynamism with a littany of players boasting youthful exuberance, sprinkled with the experience of the ever-reliable Lewis Dunk and the resurgent Pascal Gross. Crucially, they have a top, motivated manager hellbent on breaking the mould.

Upon return from the break Brighton travel a stubborn Hull side, for their first ever top flight meeting between the two sides.

Brighton have been truly sensational in the opening ten games but can they keep this up going into the notoriously tough winter period

It seems that after nearly 18 months at Liverpool Florian Wirtz is finally beginning to perform.

After a dismal first year in England in which he only registered nine goals and assists in 33 Premier League games the £116million man is starting to rediscover the form that earned him that valuation.

He enjoyed possibly his best performance in a red shirt just before the break, scoring and assisting in a 3-1 away win against Crystal Palace, and has taken that form into his international performances.

The attacking midfielder got one against Serbia in a routine 3-1 win as well as netting a brace in a 5-0 drubbing of the Netherlands - with one of his strikes an absolute pearler.

The Kop will hope this is the precursor to Wirtz seriously hitting form in the Premier League but the 23-year-old still has a lot to do before he repays the money Liverpool paid for him last year.

Florian Wirtz looks in the mood after a couple of excellent performances for Germany under ex-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp

There is no skirting around the biggest story of the international break - the psychodrama at Manchester United. The two-week break saw the Red Devils wave goodbye to Michael Carrick and say hello to Mauricio Pochettino, hoping the incoming Argentinian will inspire a much-needed turnaround.

After an emotional press conference in which he said goodbye to the US men’s national team, who he has managed for the last two years, the former Spurs and Chelsea boss is tasked with getting his new club out of the relegation places and finding some much-needed stability.

And it will be a baptism of fire for the 54-year-old, who takes his strugglers to the Anfield cauldron on Sunday, to face a Liverpool side who will have to travel to Anfield, to face a Liverpool side already 10 points ahead.

Factor in the history and rivalry this fixture holds and we are in for a cracker on Merseyside. The smart money would be on Liverpool but as we have seen so many times before a new manager bounce can transform a team in a matter of hours.

And that is all he will have to prepare his charges for their trip to Liverpool - with the new boss landing in Manchester on Wednesday morning to begin work straightaway. Welcome back, Pochettino.

Poch is back and this time in red but he will have his work cut out for him managing a dysfunctional United side currently sat in 18th

#1537. Kean’s new tibia injury rules former Juventus striker out of Como v Juventus

Moise Kean has broken down again in Como training, three weeks after treatment that was meant to fix his shin. The former Juventus striker is set to miss about two more months, so he will not face his old club on 29 November.

Moise Kean has suffered a new tibia injury in training with Como. The former Juventus striker is now undergoing further medical tests. Sky Sport Italia reported that he will be out for about two more months. That timeline rules him out of Como’s home game against Juventus.

Como’s statement of 17 November gave no recovery date. The club promised an update once more information was available.

The new problem follows a treatment that was meant to end his shin trouble. On 30 October, Como’s update described his treatment at the Cugat Institute in Barcelona as successful. The club put his recovery at about five weeks. His progress was to be reviewed every day.

That plan has now collapsed. Kean had been out since early October. The original injury came while he was playing for Italy against France on 2 October. That match was the first leg of a Nations League tie.

The setback is a heavy blow for Como. In Serie A, his outings for the club added up to 160 minutes. He has yet to score, including in his single Champions League game. He joined from Fiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent. At Fiorentina he scored 27 league goals in two seasons, 19 of them in 2024/25. Before that, he came through the Juventus academy.

Without him, Como will have to rely on Douvikas up front. The club may also look for a striker in January.

For Juventus, the news removes one threat from a crucial stretch. Como are their next opponents after Venezia. The game is the Sunday evening fixture a week later, in round 13 of Serie A. Kick-off is at 20:45.

Como 1907 is pleased to announce the signing of Italian international forward Moise Kean from @acffiorentina on an initial loan, with an obligation to make the move permanent.

Luciano Spalletti’s side need results. Juventus sit six points behind fourth place and have averaged just over 1.6 points per game, according to Corriere dello Sport. The paper sees the run of fixtures as decisive for the push for a Champions League place. It warns that dropping points against Venezia would force Juventus to win every remaining game of 2026 to stay in touch with the top four.

The schedule offers little respite after the trip to Como. Juventus host Udinese on 6 December and Monza on 14 December. They then travel to Roma on 19 December.

#1536. Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand–receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an age-associated neurodegenerative disease affecting millions worldwide, with a prevalence of roughly 10–30% among individuals older than 65 years3. Although its cardinal feature is cognitive impairment, AD manifests as a systemic condition involving profound disruptions in sleep, circadian rhythms, metabolic homeostasis, stress responses and neuroendocrine functions1. The canonical neuropathological hallmarks are extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), which alongside widespread neuroinflammation and volumetric brain changes, also intensify with ageing1,4. Because cognitive decline has traditionally guided both diagnosis and research, investigation has focused mainly on the hippocampus and cortex5. As the effects of AD on other brain regions remain poorly understood, investigating these understudied areas is crucial for elucidating the full spectrum of disease mechanisms and developing new therapeutics6.

The hypothalamus, a small but complex brain region, orchestrates a wide range of physiological and neuroendocrine processes frequently dysregulated in ageing and AD2,7. Emerging evidence suggests that hypothalamic dysfunction not only correlates with but also actively exacerbates AD pathology and cognitive decline1. Specifically, pathology within hypothalamic subregions, such as the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)8, arcuate nucleus (ARC)1,9 and mammillary body10, has been associated with prominent sleep disturbances, metabolic dysfunction and memory deficits observed in patients with AD. These systemic disruptions, in turn, are proposed to create a vicious cycle that further accelerates disease progression and cognitive decline1.

Despite its central role in homeostasis and brain ageing2,11, the hypothalamus remains an understudied region in the context of human ageing and AD. In particular, we have a limited understanding of the volumetric, cellular and molecular changes within the human hypothalamus during these processes. Although studies in animal models have highlighted hypothalamic involvement in ageing and neurodegeneration2,11,12, human studies remain scarce. This may be in part because the hypothalamus is more evolutionarily conserved than the cortex and is critical for survival, and thus it may show less overt vulnerability to ageing and prevalent diseases13. This paucity is especially pronounced for investigations that combine high-resolution imaging with single-cell analyses, complementary approaches essential for dissecting the anatomical and cellular heterogeneity of this complex brain region. This knowledge gap hinders our ability to determine how specific hypothalamic subregions and cell populations contribute to ageing and AD, and why they show differential vulnerability.

Here we present HypoAD, a multimodal atlas combining two powerful, cross-scale approaches. First, we performed high-resolution volumetric analysis of clinical imaging data from 458 individuals across the adult lifespan with varying cognitive and amyloid-β pathological statuses. Second, we generated a complementary single-cell transcriptomic atlas, comprising 614,403 nuclei from the hypothalami of 17 post-mortem donors, including young and older individuals with or without clinical and neuropathological diagnoses of AD, in which sampling was specifically enriched for the SCN, ARC and mammillary body. This dual-modality approach reveals the subregion-specific and cell-type-specific alterations of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD.

Neuroimaging studies have reported changes in hypothalamic volumes associated with ageing and cognitive decline14. Previous analyses were low-resolution or limited to major areas, masking disease-relevant subregions such as the ARC and SCN14. To overcome this limitation, we leveraged a newly developed volumetric atlas of the human hypothalamus15 to delineate and measure 13 hypothalamic and 12 extrahypothalamic structures (Supplementary Table 1). Our analysis included a clinical imaging dataset of 458 individuals across two previously described cohorts: the Adult Metabolism & Brain Resilience (AMBR) study16 (n = 202) and the Connectomics in Brain Aging and Dementia (CBA) study17 (n = 256) (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

Pearson correlation analysis revealed that whereas total hypothalamic volume showed a weak correlation with age (r = 0.15, adjusted P = 1.5 × 10 −3, Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 2), its constituent subregions showed stronger age-related correlations. Specifically, the lateral hypothalamus volume was negatively correlated with age (r = −0.22, adjusted P = 5.2 × 10−6), suggesting age-related atrophy. By contrast, the volumes of the SCN (r = 0.26, adjusted P = 2.8 × 10−8), ARC (r = 0.32, adjusted P = 1.7 × 10−11), paraventricular nucleus (r = 0.35, adjusted P = 6.9 × 10−14), periventricular nucleus (r = 0.34, adjusted P = 8.8 × 10−13) and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH) (r = 0.23, adjusted P = 1.8 × 10−6) all increased with age across all 458 individuals in two studies: AMBR and CBA (Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). A few subregions (SCN, mammillary body, dorsal periventricular nucleus and tuberomammillary nucleus) showed lower test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) < 0.4; Extended Data Fig. 1b), probably reflecting their small size and limited tissue contrast; volumetric results for these subregions should therefore be interpreted with caution. In the AMBR cohort the positive correlation between DMH volume and age was not detected in cognitively normal, amyloid-β negative individuals (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3), but it remained present in the larger harmonized two-study cohort (n = 458; Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). To test whether this age-related increase in DMH volume itself differs by disease status, an age × group interaction model (group: cognitively normal and amyloid-negative versus all others; Methods) showed no significant interaction (effect size/estimate ± standard error (s.e.) = −0.041 ± 0.025, adjusted P = 0.12, Supplementary Table 4), indicating that age-related increase in DMH volume does not differ significantly between groups. This suggests that the DM–age association probably reflects a general feature of hypothalamic ageing in this subregion—which is implicated in sleep–wakefulness18 and body-weight regulation19—rather than a process specific to neurodegeneration.

a, Pearson correlation heatmap of subregion volumes and age at MRI. Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Boxes mark five clusters (complete linkage on 1 − r). All subregions were analysed. Benjamini–Hochberg correction covers unique pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson r in pooled (black, n = 458), CBA (orange, n = 256) and AMBR (blue, n = 202) analyses. n denotes independent participants. Filled circles indicate Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 across 26 correlations per analysis. Open circles indicate non-significance. Two-sided Pearson tests in a,b. c, Age (left) and female-sex (right, male reference) effects from Gaussian identity-link models of log-volume, adjusting for age, sex, cognitive and amyloid-β status, their interaction, ICV and study (n = 316 independent participants with complete covariate data, 197 female, 119 male, CBA 209, AMBR 107). AHA, anterior hypothalamic area; DPEH, dorsal periventricular nucleus; HYPO, hypothalamus; LH, lateral hypothalamus; MM, mammillary body; MPO, medial preoptic nucleus; NS, not significant; Pa, paraventricular nucleus; Pe, periventricular nucleus; PH, posterior hypothalamus; s.d., standard deviation; SO, supraoptic nucleus; TM, tuberomammillary nucleus; VM, ventromedial nucleus.

In a generalized linear model (GLM) controlling for biological sex, intracranial volume (ICV), cognitive status and amyloid-β pathology, lateral hypothalamus volume decreased with age (effect size/estimate ± s.e. = −0.021 ± 0.0064, adjusted P = 0.0019). The SCN (0.059 ± 0.018, adjusted P = 0.0029), ARC (0.058 ± 0.012, adjusted P = 4.2 × 10−6), paraventricular nucleus (0.14 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 1.8 × 10−11), periventricular nucleus (0.092 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 6.4 × 10−6), DMH (0.055 ± 0.016, adjusted P = 0.0011) and total hypothalamic volumes (0.022 ± 0.0071, adjusted P = 0.0048) showed a positive association with age (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). Biological sex was also a significant factor: females showed smaller volumes in several subregions, most prominently in the supraoptic nucleus (−0.097 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 1.7 × 10−6) (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). This aligns with previous studies emphasizing the sexually dimorphic nature of the hypothalamus, including the supraoptic nucleus2,14. As expected, most subregion volumes were positively correlated with ICV (Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). For comparison, volumes of most extrahypothalamic structures showed age-related reductions, smaller sex differences than the hypothalamus and positive correlations with ICV (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 4). Representative subregions were reconstructed in three dimensions (Fig. 1d).

To holistically evaluate volumetric relationships, we performed principal component analysis (PCA) on volumetric data from all 25 delineated hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). The first two principal components (PCs) were primarily associated with age, sex and global scaling factors (intracranial and total brain volume), along which individuals separated (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Amyloid-β and cognitive status showed weaker associations with these components, and after residualizing for age, sex and global scaling factors, neither remained significantly associated with the leading PCs (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). This indicates that disease status does not define an independent dominant axis of macrostructural variation, and that the more sensitive disease-associated signal may instead be captured at the molecular level.

Examination of volumetric trajectories by means of scatter plots stratified by cognitive and amyloid-β status revealed subregion-specific patterns that also differed by sex (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Notably, individuals with AD (defined as cognitive decline and amyloid-β positivity) showed reduced total hypothalamus and lateral hypothalamus volumes compared with their age-matched non-AD counterparts, consistent with the overall age-related decline of these regions (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, ARC, SCN, paraventricular nucleus, periventricular nucleus and DMH volumes were increased in individuals with AD relative to age-matched non-AD individuals (Extended Data Fig. 3g). This pattern did not reach statistical significance, potentially reflecting the insensitivity of volumetric measures to the relatively early disease stage and the limited sample size (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Subregion volumes classified cognitive status, amyloid-β status and AD better than total hypothalamic volume (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), suggesting that subregion-specific volumetric changes capture disease-relevant variation that is obscured when the hypothalamus is treated as a single structure.

Thus, ageing is associated with subregion-specific volumetric changes that persist after controlling for amyloid-β and cognition, whereas AD-linked changes did not reach significance, motivating a complementary, higher-resolution molecular modality.

Volumetric data provide anatomical context but cannot reveal cell-type-specific molecular changes. We therefore performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on post-mortem hemi-hypothalamus tissue from 14 individuals (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a): seven with mostly early-stage AD (n = 6 sporadic, n = 1 familial) and seven age-matched, cognitively and neuropathologically normal control participants. The familial AD sample (AD_44, ID 7A in Fig. 2b; APOE4/4) was excluded from all differential analyses and retained as an extreme example of advanced pathology.

a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Frozen post-mortem hypothalamic tissue from 14 individuals (7 non-AD control participants and 7 patients with AD (6 age-matched sporadic and 1 younger familial)) was macrodissected to enrich for the ARC, SCN and mammillary nucleus (MN) subregions. Nuclei were isolated, and libraries were prepared and sequenced on a NovaSeq platform. The resulting data were integrated with 133,879 publicly available nuclei from three young, healthy control participants, yielding a final dataset of 614,403 nuclei across young control, older control (non-AD) and AD groups for comparative analysis. b, Overview of the 14 individuals included in the snRNA-seq study, detailing sample IDs, clinical condition (non-AD control, early-stage AD or familial AD), age at death and Braak stage. Each individual contributed tissue from three hypothalamic subregions (ARC, SCN and MN), totalling 42 tissue samples processed across seven experimental batches. c, UMAP plot of the integrated 614,403 nuclei. Distinct clusters represent identified main cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, fibroblasts, epithelial cells, OPCs and leukocytes. Each cell type is annotated and highlighted with a unique colour. d, Dot plot of selected marker genes. Dot size corresponds to the fraction of cells within a given cell type expressing the marker; colour intensity indicates the average normalized expression level. e, Normalized expression of key canonical marker genes mapped onto the UMAP plot from c. Representative markers include GFAP (astrocytes), FLT1 (endothelial cells), CFAP299 (ependymal cells), TTR (epithelial cells), C1QA (microglia), PTPRC/CD45 (leukocytes), SYT1 (neurons), MBP (oligodendrocytes), VCAN (OPCs) and COL1A1 (fibroblasts). Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Yu, D. https://biorender.com/zt57wnj (2026).

Donors with AD predominantly had sporadic, clinically confirmed cognitive decline with pathology (Braak stage IV; Fig. 2b), a stage optimal for detecting transcriptional changes while neuronal populations remain20. Hierarchical clustering grouped samples by pathology status rather than by confounders such as time of death or quality metrics (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

For annotation, we integrated our dataset with 133,879 previously published, high-quality human hypothalamic nuclei from three younger individuals (29, 42 and 50 years of age)21,22 using the single-cell variational inference algorithm23. Main cell types were identified through the expression of canonical marker genes (Fig. 2c–e and quality control in Extended Data Fig. 4b–g).

To identify transcriptomic features distinguishing hypothalamic cells from patients with AD versus control individuals, we trained Elastic Net models on 36,600 genes from 480,524 cells. The dataset spanned seven independent batches, each containing one donor with AD and one control donor (Fig. 3a). This balanced design enabled a leave-one-batch-out cross-validation that yielded strong classification performance for both the all-cell model and cell-type-specific models for the main cell types (Fig. 3b).

a, Nested leave-one-batch-out cross-validation. Outer folds held out one batch for testing. Inner folds selected hyperparameters using the remaining batches. Each of seven nonoverlapping batches contained two distinct donors (one control, one AD): 480,524 cells × 36,600 genes. b, Receiver-operating-characteristic curves for Elastic Net models using all nuclei (all-cell model) and each of the five most abundant cell types. Area under the curve reflects pooled performance across seven outer folds. The dashed line indicates chance (area under the curve of 0.5). c, Top 20 AD-predictive genes per model ranked by absolute model weight within each outer fold. Bars show mean rank across folds, ordered from highest importance (lowest rank). Error bars show s.d. (upper side shown), and dots show individual fold ranks. Seven all-cell ranks greater than 300 appear as triangles at the axis limit. Fully coloured and pale bars indicate positive and negative weights, respectively. n = 7 outer folds per model, with overlapping training sets. Folds are resampling units, not biological replicates. Each held-out batch contains two independent donors, totalling 14 donors. Models used 480,524 nuclei (all-cell), 227,283 oligodendrocytes, 103,815 neurons, 57,437 astrocytes, 52,390 microglia and 22,004 OPCs from these 14 donors. d, Top 35 shared features. Bars show mean rank across all five cell-type-specific models, with lower ranks indicating higher importance. e, Top 15 features per cell type, selected by gene rank in the target versus other cell types. Bars show specificity scores. f, Selected significantly enriched KEGG pathways from GSEA of genes ranked by signed model weights, for all-cell and cell-type-specific models. The x axis shows absolute normalized enrichment score, dot size indicates pathway gene count and colour indicates significance (−log10[FDR]). Astro., astrocyte; AUC, area under the curve; NES, normalized enrichment score; Oligo., oligodendrocyte.

Averaging absolute gene weights across the seven outer cross-validation folds gave the top 20 features per classifier (Fig. 3c), many previously implicated in AD pathology, lending biological support to our model’s predictions. The all-cell model’s top features included arginine–vasopressin (encoded by AVP), a circadian neuropeptide elevated in AD24. Cell-type-specific models likewise highlighted AD-linked genes: MCF2L (differentially methylated in AD; oligodendrocyte)25, ARL17B (an inhibitory neuron expression quantitative trait locus elevated in AD cortex; neurons)26, CHI3L1 (astrocyte-secreted neuroinflammation marker and a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker for early AD diagnosis; astrocytes)27, RNF150 (a cis-expression quantitative trait locus, microglia)28 and ITGA8 (linked to demyelination; oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC))29 (Fig. 3c).

Ranking genes by mean rank across the five most abundant cell types identified HP1BP3 as the top shared feature (Fig. 3d), a candidate modulator of hippocampal cognitive ageing affected by metformin30,31 but underexplored in the hypothalamus. A per-gene specificity rank (Fig. 3e) revealed strong enrichment of long noncoding RNAs (for example, LINC02646, LINC00551, LINC01250, LINC00937 and LINC02389) among top neuronal features (Fig. 3e), providing a cell-type-specific resource of known and new AD-associated genes. Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on the ranked predictive genes revealed a significant enrichment for circadian rhythm and inflammatory pathways (Fig. 3f, Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 5), connecting our cell-level classifiers to established hallmarks of neurodegeneration.

We next performed pseudobulk differential expression analysis (edgeR likelihood-ratio test (LRT), by cell type and sample) between early-AD and control samples (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6). Notably, microglia showed the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), highlighting their substantial transcriptional response even in early AD.
